strengths: The LaRI representation is a simple, well-motivated formulation: predicting depth-ordered, view-aligned layered point maps plus a ray stopping index turns unseen-surface reasoning into a standard 2D regression problem, avoiding per-point querying, grid costs, or multi-iteration pipelines of prior amodal/CUT3R-style approaches.

Strong and efficient empirical results: on object-level GSO, the method matches or beats TRELLIS in the view-aligned setting while using ~4% of the training objects and ~17.5% of the parameters, and is an order of magnitude faster (Table 5); on scene-level SCRREAM it enables unseen-region reasoning in a single feed-forward pass with competitive overall scores.
The proposed ray stopping index formulation is a sensible solution to the ordered-mask problem and is validated against direct binary segmentation (Table 6), showing large gains in mIoU/DICE.

A substantial and non-trivial data curation pipeline (Objaverse filtering of internal structures, 3D-FRONT room splitting, ScanNet++ rendering, Blender/Pytorch3D coordination) is described in enough detail to be genuinely useful to the community, and the authors commit to releasing data, pipeline, and evaluation scripts, which addresses the currently non-standardized comparisons in this area.

Comprehensive ablations covering layer count, pre-trained weights, mask prediction strategy, and efficiency; the limitations section is honest and specific (low point density on ray-parallel surfaces, sensitivity to limited observation, dataset scale/diversity).
weaknesses: The claim of 'completeness' is overstated: layered ray intersections only recover surfaces intersected by camera rays; geometry outside the ray bundle or far behind the visible surface is structurally unrepresentable, and the fixed layer count L inherently caps the representable scene complexity (the L=3 vs L=5 ablation shows a large sensitivity gap on objects, suggesting brittle behavior for complex objects).

Scene-level results are mixed: the method is clearly inferior on visible surfaces to MoGe (FS@0.05 0.589 vs 0.786) and only 'comparable' overall, and the dual evaluation settings ('Ours*' vs 'Ours' with region-specific sampling) introduce flexibility in how the comparison is presented that reviewers must trust; the test set is small (460 images from a single dataset).

Unseen geometry from a single view is fundamentally ambiguous, and a deterministic regression target penalizes plausible-but-not-GT completions; the paper acknowledges this but does not quantify how sensitive the Chamfer/F-score comparisons are to this mismatch, and does not discuss the alternative of stochastic/generative heads within the same representation.

Two separate ViT-Large backbones (LaRI map + ray stopping index) and two separately trained models (object vs. scene) undercut the 'unified' framing; the additional mask model is not counted in the efficiency comparison of Table 5.

Presentation/consistency issues: the ViT backbone is cited as [75], which in the reference list is the SSIM paper (Wang et al.), not Dosovitskiy et al.; MoGe is cited inconsistently as [72]/[73] in Table 5; minor notation slips (e.g., 'v̂pred ∈ V̂pred' where V̂pred is defined as a set).

The scale-shift alignment used in both training loss and evaluation conflates metric and relative reasoning, making it hard to tell whether the learned layers are metrically meaningful, which matters for the stated robotics/VR applications.

strengths: The core idea of predicting depth-ordered, layered point maps (a 'reverse LDI') for unseen geometry from a single image is clean and intuitive, and the ray stopping index formulation is a sensible way to handle variable numbers of intersections with a single per-pixel ordinal prediction.

The paper covers both object-level (GSO) and scene-level (SCRREAM) evaluation with standard 3D metrics (CD, F-score at multiple thresholds), and includes a fairly thorough set of ablations (number of layers, pre-trained weights, mask prediction strategy, efficiency), which is more than many submissions provide.

The data curation pipeline (Objaverse filtering, 3D-FRONT room splitting, ScanNet++ rendering, coordinating Blender/Pytorch3D) addresses a genuine practical obstacle, and the authors promise to release the benchmark and evaluation scripts, which would be a community contribution given the current lack of standardized evaluation in this area.
Efficiency results (Table 5) are compelling: ~31 ms inference with ~314M parameters versus 700–900 ms and 1–2B parameters for TRELLIS/SPAR3D, while achieving competitive geometry quality.

The limitations section is honest and specific, identifying layered-representation artifacts (low point density for ray-parallel surfaces) and the sensitivity of a deterministic approach under heavy occlusion.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty for a machine learning venue: the approach is standard supervised regression with a ViT-Large backbone and a DPT-style decoder, plus a separate ViT-Large classifier for the stopping index. The contribution is primarily a representation and data-engineering effort rather than a new learning technique; the related layered depth image / multi-plane image literature is acknowledged but the delta over these prior representations is not sharply argued.

Evaluation fairness concerns. Object-level comparisons are against models trained on very different data scales (16K objects vs 500K for TRELLIS), so 'comparable to a generative model with 4% of the data' conflates model capacity, data, and representation effects without a controlled comparison (e.g., TRELLIS-scale training or a matched-data baseline). In the view-aligned setting, the proposed method is structurally advantaged (its output is natively camera-aligned, while competitors must register via ICP), which partly explains the large FS@0.02 gains and weakens the headline claim of outperforming TRELLIS.

The scene-level protocol is ambiguous and potentially favorable: 'Ours' uses region-specific point sampling while 'Ours*' uses a fixed point set, and the choice between them materially changes the visible-surface numbers (FS@0.05 0.589 vs 0.510). The rationale for which setting matches competing methods is only briefly stated; on visible surfaces the method is clearly worse than MoGe, and the 'overall' advantage rests on unseen regions where no strong baseline exists except a specially queried CUT3R.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce confidence: the text reports 341M parameters while Table 5 reports 314.2M; Table 5 cites MoGe as [73] instead of [72]; Figure 4's caption cites SCRREAM as [16] instead of [32]; the L=3 ablation shows an anomalously large degradation on GSO (CD 0.072 vs 0.025) that is not explained.

Two separate ViT-Large networks are used (point map regression + ray stopping index), but the efficiency analysis in Table 5 appears to report only the point-map model's parameters/time; the total system cost relative to single-network baselines is therefore unclear.

Reproducibility is only prospective: no code or data is available at submission time, all releases are promised ('will be released'), and several critical evaluation details (exact ICP brute-force search procedure, sampling protocols) are described only at a high level.

The scale-shift-aligned (non-metric) formulation is presented as appropriate, but the paper does not discuss when metric reasoning is required, and the shift-only-in-z restriction of Eq. (3) is not justified.

strengths: The core idea—reversing the classic layered depth image (LDI) concept to *predict* all depth-ordered ray-surface intersections from a single image—is clean, well-motivated, and yields a view-aligned, complete geometric representation that unifies object- and scene-level unseen-geometry reasoning. This is a genuinely new angle on a recognized problem.

The ray stopping index formulation (Sec. 3.3) is an elegant solution to the ordered-mask prediction problem, and the authors support its design choice with a direct ablation (Table 6) against binary mask regression.

The data curation pipeline (Sec. 3.4) is a substantial engineering contribution: filtering internal artifacts in Objaverse assets, splitting house-level meshes into rooms, and coordinating Blender/Pytorch3D conventions for ground-truth LaRI rendering. This addresses a real obstacle for future work and will be released with the evaluation benchmark.

Evaluation is reasonably broad and multi-faceted: canonical vs. view-aligned ground truth on GSO, visible/unseen/overall splits on SCRREAM, ablations over layer count, pre-training weights, mask prediction strategy, and efficiency comparisons. The efficiency results (314M params, 31.5ms) are convincing.

The paper is honest about limitations (Fig. 5): sparse points on ray-parallel surfaces, deterministic failure under heavy occlusion, and limited data diversity/scale. Limitations are discussed rather than hidden.

Claims are mostly carefully scoped: the paper explicitly concedes inferiority to TRELLIS under canonical GT and to MoGe on visible surfaces, and attributes the view-aligned win to representation advantages rather than raw model capacity.
weaknesses: The efficiency accounting appears incomplete: two separate ViT-Large backbones are trained (point map model plus ray stopping index model, Sec. 3.2-3.3), but Table 5 and the abstract's parameter claims (314M / 341M) seem to count only one network. Total inference cost and parameters for the full system should be clarified, as the headline '17% of parameters' comparisons could be overstated.

The method is fundamentally limited to surfaces intersectable by camera rays; concave/enclosed structures fully occluded in every direction or geometry deviating strongly along the ray receive no support (acknowledged, but this bounds applicability for robotics downstream uses the paper motivates in the introduction).

The scene-level gains are modest: 'Ours' underperforms MoGe on visible surfaces and its overall advantage comes mainly from the unseen-region capability; the strongest unseen-geometry baselines (AmodalDepth, full CUT3R variants) are excluded or evaluated only in a reference configuration (iter-5 with five virtual poses), so the scene-level comparison is not exhaustive.

The jump in ablation results from L=3 to L=5 on GSO (CD 0.072→0.025, FS 0.894) is large and unexplained; it is unclear whether L=3 training was disadvantaged by capacity, supervision weighting, or mask/hit ratio artifacts, which slightly undermines confidence in the reported default configuration.

The representation is relative (scale-shift aligned), not metric; the paper motivates collision avoidance and robotics applications, but metric ambiguity may limit those uses, and this tension is not discussed.

Reproducibility currently depends on promised releases (pipeline, benchmark, scripts); several baseline details (ICP parameters, private test splits of prior work) are acknowledged as uncontrollable, which is honest but means quantitative comparisons cannot be fully verified at review time.

Fixed maximum layer count L is a hard design constraint; variable-intersection-count modeling (e.g., per-pixel unbounded depth) is dismissed but alternatives within the layered paradigm are not explored.

strengths: Simple and well-motivated formulation: recasting occluded-geometry reasoning as multi-layer point map regression (LDI-inspired) with a ray stopping index is elegant, view-aligned, and runs in a single feed-forward pass, unifying object-level and scene-level tasks.

Substantial data contribution: an annotation pipeline over five public datasets (synthetic and real) with filtering, coordinate-convention handling, and layer-coverage statistics (Fig. 6) that justify the choice of L=5; the promised release of the pipeline improves reproducibility.

Comprehensive evaluation: two GT regimes (canonical vs. view-aligned) for object-level results, separate reporting of visible/unseen/overall regions at scene level, and thorough ablations (number of layers, pre-training weights, stopping index vs. binary mask, shared vs. separate encoders, per-layer accuracy, point map vs. depth map output).
Favorable efficiency: fewer parameters and faster inference than generative competitors (TRELLIS, SPAR3D, SF3D), making the approach practically attractive.

Honest limitations section that correctly identifies inherent weaknesses (sparse points on surfaces parallel to camera rays, deterministic averaging on ambiguous occlusions, synthetic-to-real domain gap).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: layered depth/intersection representations are well established (LDIs, MPIs, MLD, Slice3D), and the core contribution is a supervised regression of these layers using standard ViT-Large + DINO/MoGe pre-trained backbones; the ray stopping index is a sensible but straightforward ordinal classification.

Predicting unseen geometry from a single image is fundamentally ill-posed, yet the paper treats it as pure deterministic regression; the evaluation cannot distinguish geometric faithfulness from easy-to-guess completions (e.g., floors, walls behind furniture), which plausibly inflate unseen-region F-scores. No comparison against generative/uncertainty-aware alternatives on unseen-region quality.

Scene-level evaluation is partially in-domain: the model is trained on 3D-FRONT and evaluated on a held-out 3D-FRONT subset; the real-world evaluation (SCRREAM) is very small (11 scenes, 460 images), weakening claims of real-world generalization.

Mixed scene-level results: on SCRREAM, visible-surface accuracy is clearly worse than MoGe (FS@0.05 0.589 vs. 0.786), so the 'overall' advantage rests largely on coverage of unseen regions rather than better geometry.

The two-backbone design (separate ViT-Large encoders for point map and stopping index) doubles parameters to 620M; the absolute mask quality (mIoU ~0.56) is modest, and only a weak binary-mask baseline is compared in Table 7.

Presentation issues undermine polish: e.g., 'ViT-Large (Wang et al., 2004)' is a clearly wrong citation, duplicated/incorrect citations for DINOv2/DINOv3 in Table 5, typos ('Seperate', 'It inferences of'), and repeated rows in Table 6.

No downstream-task evaluation (navigation, planning, collision avoidance) despite motivating unseen-geometry reasoning with robotics/AR applications, so the practical utility of the extra layers remains demonstrated only by reconstruction metrics.

strengths: The LaRI representation is simple and well-motivated: reformulating layered depth images as view-aligned layered point maps enables a single feed-forward pass for both visible and occluded geometry, which is a useful capability absent from standard depth/point-map models.

The ray-stopping index formulation is a sensible, well-argued solution to the ordered-mask problem, and the ablation (Table 7) convincingly shows it outperforms direct binary mask regression (mIoU 0.56 vs 0.09 on GSO).

The annotation pipeline over five datasets (synthetic and real) and the coverage analysis (Fig. 6) provide a reusable evaluation benchmark for a task that previously lacked data, and the authors state they will release the pipeline.

The paper is generally well written with a clear method section, extensive ablations (layer count, pre-trained weights, shared vs. separate encoders, point maps vs. depth maps, per-layer accuracy), an honest limitations section, and an appropriate impact statement.
Efficiency results (Table 6) are meaningful: ~5-13x faster inference than generative baselines with far fewer parameters.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core idea is layered depth images (Shade et al., 1998) applied as multi-output regression; the closest prior, MLD (Shin et al., 2019), already performs multi-layer depth prediction for scene reconstruction and is cited but never compared against. The delta over prior LDI-based work is largely the point-map output and the stopping-index head, which is incremental.

The real-world scene results undercut the headline claims. On SCRREAM (real data), LaRI is clearly worse than MoGe in every region (visible CD 0.057 vs 0.035, FS 0.589 vs 0.786; overall FS 0.590 vs 0.668), and its 'unseen' advantage mostly materializes on synthetic 3D-FRONT. Combined with the admitted synthetic-heavy training data and domain gap, the evidence for practical unseen-geometry reasoning on real scenes is weak.

Per-layer results (Table 9) show severe degradation for occluded layers (e.g., SCRREAM FS@0.05 drops from 0.588 to ~0.36-0.43), and Fig. 4/8 show hallucinated or misaligned unseen surfaces; deterministic regression of under-constrained occluded geometry is a fundamental limitation that the paper under-addresses beyond a brief limitations note.

The evaluation protocol partially favors the proposed method: the view-aligned GT comparison is naturally advantageous for a view-aligned regression method, and competing unseen-geometry baselines (KYN, DRDF, Rayst3R, AmodalDepth) are excluded from the main scene comparison; CUT3R is evaluated with noise-perturbed virtual poses, a setup that is hard to judge as fair.

The object-level 'comparable to TRELLIS with 10x fewer parameters and 10x faster inference' claim is selective: TRELLIS substantially outperforms LaRI under canonical GT (FS@0.02: 0.611 vs 0.601, CD 0.027 vs 0.029), and it is a generative model with different goals; LaRI is also worse than TRELLIS at every object-level metric in Table 2.

Presentation sloppiness that undermines confidence: ViT-Large is attributed to 'Wang et al., 2004' (an image-quality paper) in multiple places, DINOv3 is cited as 'Oquab et al., 2023' in Table 5, Table 6 duplicates the 'Ours' rows for the scene section, and there are typos ('Seperate', 'inferences of all ray intersections', confusing phrasing such as 'RGB-D scans than images').

No statistical significance, variance, or cross-seed reporting for the quantitative results, and the ray-stopping-index model doubles the backbone, which weakens the efficiency narrative relative to single-backbone baselines like MoGe.

strengths: The core idea—reformulating single-view occluded geometry estimation as multi-layer ray-intersection point map regression (an LDI-inspired formulation) with a ray-stopping index for validity—is simple, well-motivated, and yields a view-aligned output that supports both object- and scene-level reconstruction in one feed-forward pass.

The paper makes a substantive systems contribution beyond the model: a complete annotation pipeline over five datasets (synthetic and real: Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, GSO, SCRREAM), with detailed documentation of coordinate-convention pitfalls and planned release of the data generation code, which improves reproducibility and community value.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: two GT regimes (canonical vs. view-aligned), separate reporting for visible/unseen/overall regions at scene level, ablations on layer count, pre-training, output representation, and encoder sharing, plus a per-layer accuracy analysis (Table 9) that honestly quantifies degradation under heavier occlusion.

The proposed method is competitive empirically: it outperforms image-supervised object reconstruction baselines (SF3D, SPAR3D) with notable margins and, in view-aligned evaluation, beats TRELLIS by 6% FS@0.02 while being ~14x faster and ~3x smaller in parameters (Tables 2 and 6).
The ray-stopping index formulation is a sensible ordinal alternative to direct binary mask regression, and the ablation (Table 7) shows a large empirical gain supporting this design choice.

The limitations section is candid and specific (point-density artifacts on ray-parallel surfaces, deterministic failure under ambiguous occlusion, synthetic domain gap), and the impact statement discusses appropriate deployment safeguards.
weaknesses: The paper treats prediction of unobservable occluded geometry as pure regression, without any uncertainty or confidence modeling beyond the ray-stopping index. For genuinely invisible surfaces, a deterministic model must hallucinate; the reported unseen-region metrics could mask substantial ambiguity, and the qualitative limitations (Fig. 5) only begin to quantify this.

The scene-level evaluation of unseen geometry is comparatively thin: SCRREAM has only 11 scenes / 460 images, 3D-FRONT is synthetic and shares the same rendering pipeline as training, and CUT3R with iteratively noised virtual poses is a somewhat indirect proxy for the unseen-geometry competition. Stronger baselines from semantic scene completion or Rayst3R/AmodalDepth-style methods (even with their extra inputs) would strengthen the central claim.

Evaluation protocol choices may favor the proposed method: predictions and GT are aligned via the same scale-shift fitting used in training (Eq. 4), and the canonical-GT comparison relies on a brute-force rotation search plus ICP whose adequacy for view-unaligned generative baselines is acknowledged but not verified (e.g., no sensitivity analysis to the 1000-angle search resolution).

The fixed maximum layer count L=5, while ablated, caps the method's expressiveness for scenes with deep occlusion stacks; the authors' own coverage analysis (Fig. 6) shows non-trivial mass beyond 5 layers for 3D-FRONT and ScanNet++, yet per-layer results (Table 9) already show notable degradation by layers 2-5.

Minor presentation issues undermine polish: e.g., ViT-Large is cited as (Wang et al., 2004) (an image-quality paper) in Secs. 3.2 and 3.3, and 'Seperate' appears in the appendix heading; Table 6 duplicates the 'Ours' rows under both object- and scene-level comparisons in a way that is easy to misread.

The binary-segmentation baseline in Table 7 (mIoU 0.091 on GSO) is suspiciously low relative to the stopping-index result (0.560); without implementation details for this baseline, it is unclear whether the comparison is fully fair.

No quantitative evaluation is provided on ScanNet++ despite it being part of the training pipeline and discussed in the appendix, leaving real-world generalization measured mainly on the small SCRREAM set.
